content.title: About
content.content: Jicama is an edible root vegetable belonging to the legume family (Pachyrhizus erosus). Native to Mexico and Central America, it is now cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. It has a crisp, juicy texture and a mildly sweet flavor reminiscent of apple and radish. Jicama is typically eaten raw, sliced thin for salads, snacks, or as a crunchy component in vegetable dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “jicama” comes from the Mexican word “xicama,” meaning “root.”
The vegetable is over 90 % water, making it a very low‑calorie food.
Unlike most legumes, properly cultivated jicama does not contain toxic glycosides.
In traditional Mexican cuisine, jicama is served with lime, salt, and chili.
Only the thick, smooth root is edible; the leaves and stems are usually discarded.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 20 mg of vitamin C, supporting immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup of sliced jicama (≈130 g) contains only about 45 kcal, making it ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart health.

items.title: Contains inulin
items.content: Inulin is a prebiotic fiber that feeds beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience an allergy to jicama.

items.title: Foodborne illness if stored improperly
items.content: When kept warm for extended periods, the root can rot and foster bacterial growth.

items.title: Digestive difficulty for young children
items.content: Due to its high fiber content, small children should receive only small, well‑cut pieces.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Jicama is usually washed, optionally peeled, and cut into thin strips or cubes. It can be added to salads, salsas, fresh juices, or used as a crunchy garnish for meat dishes. A light sprinkle of salt and a squeeze of lime juice enhance its flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store jicama in the refrigerator, wrapped in a plastic bag or placed in an airtight container. Properly refrigerated, it stays fresh for 2–3 weeks. Discard any pieces that become soft, develop spots, or emit an off‑odor.
